newsitem.title: USA: Stocks lose more ground as bond interest rates rise again.
newsitem.headline: Stocks lose more ground as bond interest rates rise again.

text.p: Stock prices closed lower on Thursday as Wall Street's nerves were again rattled by another rise in long-term bond interest rates ahead of next week's meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
Worries about the quality of second-quarter corporate profits also cut into stocks, analysts said.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 35.73 points lower at 7,654.25.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,455 to 1,300 on heavy volume of 499 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

It was the fourth day this week that stocks were subject to sharp swings. On Monday, the Dow had its second-biggest point loss ever as it shed 192 points, followed by Tuesday's gut-wrenching recovery of 154 points and Wednesday's 68-point fall.
Since the beginning of May, the blue-chip Dow index has risen nearly 700 points, or 9.7 percent, fostering doubts about whether the run-up still had staying power.
"People are nervous as cats out there and they are doing some selling to nail down profits," said Marshall Acuff, chief investment strategest for Smith Barney.
Analysts said stocks were jarred by the steady rise in long-term interest rates, which have gone up for four straight days.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 17/32, raising its yield to 6.78 percent from 6.74 percent Wednesday. The price and yield move in opposite directions.

"Yields have backed up here above 6.77 percent. A combination of that, plus portfolio juggling, and many feel we've had a monstrous run and stocks need to consolidate," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
More warnings of lower second-quarter profits from technology company Komag Inc. also cooled investors' thirst for stocks, analysts said.

"For the past three quarters, there has been a sense of hesitancy and nervousness in the month before earnings get reported when profit warnings come out. We are heading into the reporting period, and this quarter shouldn't be any different," Acuff said.

Wall Street was also on edge -- as is traditional -- ahead of the meeting next Tuesday and Wednesday of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, although most economists are not expecting a credit tightening until the panel's August meeting.
Bleier said that despite the volatility, he remained bullish short-term.
"You have to take these sell-offs with a grain of salt. We are taking a pause, but the fundamental macroeconomic backdrop remains unchanged," he said.
The stocks of computer disk drive companies slumped after San Jose, Calif.-based Komag said its profits for the second quarter and the rest of the year would fall short of Wall Street expectations.
The stock, the most heavily traded on Nasdaq, fell 6-14/16 to 16-11/16. Rival disk drive makers Seagate Technology was off 1/2 at 33-1/2 and Read-Rite Corp. lost 2-2/16 to 20-1/16.

Technology and drug stocks, which have led the market higher recently, lost ground. Pharmacia & Upjohn shed 11/16 to 34-1/16, Johnson & Johnson fell 1-5/16 to 63-7/8 and Warner-Lambert Co. was off 2-3/4 at 119.

Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc. surged 11-9/16 to 91 after its French parent company, Rhone-Poulenc SA, said it was considering launching a $4.3 billion bid to buy the rest of Rhone-Poulenc Rorer it does not own.
The Nasdaq Composite index lost 9.86 points to 1,436.38.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 5.31 to 883.68. The American Stock Exchange index was off 3.14 to 616.10.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.97 to 460.93. The average share was down 19 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at 8,364.369, down 42.835, or 0.51 percent.
